KLA Corporation (NASDAQ: KLAC) is the undisputed market leader in semiconductor process control, holding an estimated 55–60 percent share of the global inspection and metrology equipment market and approximately 75–80 percent of patterned-wafer defect inspection — a competitive position accumulated over five decades and defended by physics-intensive tool architectures, a proprietary installed-base intelligence loop, and a services franchise that reached $2.5 billion in annual revenue across fifty consecutive quarters of growth by fiscal 2025.

First, the AI infrastructure build-out has created a step-change in leading-edge-node demand at TSMC, Samsung Foundry, and advanced DRAM manufacturers, and KLA's process control intensity — units of inspection required per wafer — rises disproportionately as logic shrinks toward gate-all-around and as memory manufacturers stack NAND layers deeper. chapters.title: The Process Control Monopolist: KLA's Strategic Position at the AI Infrastructure Inflection
chapters.body:
## A Wafer in the Dark Field

At TSMC's gigafab in Hsinchu, a 300-millimetre silicon wafer carrying gate-all-around nanosheet transistors at the 2-nanometre node enters the darkened enclosure of a KLA Broadband Plasma inspection tool. The tool floods the patterned surface with a broadband plasma light source, collects scattered photons across multiple angles simultaneously, and compares the signal map against a reference die — the entire sequence executed in seconds, repeated hundreds of times across the wafer surface, generating a defect file that feeds directly into the fab's yield-management loop. Nothing moves to the next process step until that file clears. At transistor densities exceeding 100 million per square millimetre, the cost of a single escaped defect propagates geometrically; the cost of the KLA tool, by comparison, is trivial.

That physical reality — process control as structural necessity rather than optional overhead — is the foundation on which KLA Corporation built a franchise that commands approximately 75 to 80 percent of the global patterned-wafer inspection market and roughly 55 to 60 percent of the broader inspection and metrology market. Rick Wallace, who has served as President and Chief Executive Officer since January 2006 and joined the company in 1988 as an applications engineer, has spent nearly four decades at KLA watching that foundation become harder to dislodge. "We're a key enabler of the AI ecosystem," Wallace told analysts when KLA reported record quarterly revenue of $3.297 billion in the second fiscal quarter of 2026.

## Three Theses, One Franchise

This dossier traces KLA's strategic position through three interlocking narratives.

The first is the near-monopoly moat in inspection and metrology — a reinforcing loop in which tens of thousands of installed tools accumulate proprietary defect-signature databases, which sharpen recipe performance, which justify premium pricing, which fund the physics-intensive R&D necessary to stay ahead of the next node's detection requirements. No competitor has replicated this loop at scale. Applied Materials and Lam Research dominate deposition and etch; ASML owns lithography exposure; KLA owns the measurement layer that tells every other tool whether its output was acceptable.

The second narrative is the advanced-packaging revenue inflection. Hybrid-bonding pitches measured in single-digit microns and HBM memory-stack tolerances have created a back-end inspection market that barely appeared on KLA's revenue line in fiscal 2022. By fiscal 2025, revenue attributed to advanced packaging exceeded $925 million — up approximately 85 percent year over year — driven by chiplet assembly and high-bandwidth memory demand from AI-accelerator supply chains at TSMC, Samsung, SK Hynix, and their OSAT partners.

The third narrative is capital-return discipline. At the March 2026 Investor Day, management presented a 2030 target model calling for $26 billion in revenue, approximately 63.5 percent gross margin, 45 to 47 percent operating margin, and $84 in non-GAAP diluted earnings per share. The board simultaneously authorised a $7.0 billion supplemental share-repurchase programme and approved a 21 percent increase in the quarterly dividend to $2.30 per share. Those numbers are the financial architecture of a management team that views the balance sheet as optimised and prefers EPS accretion over acquisitive diversification.

## Revenue at Scale

KLA's fiscal 2025 (year ended June 30, 2025) produced total revenues of $12.16 billion, a 23.9 percent year-over-year increase from the $9.81 billion recorded in fiscal 2024, with GAAP net income of $4.06 billion and free cash flow approaching $4.4 billion. Entering fiscal 2026, the quarterly run-rate continued to accelerate: $3.21 billion in Q1, $3.297 billion in Q2, and $3.415 billion in Q3. Management guided Q4 fiscal 2026 revenue at approximately $3.35 billion, placing the full-year total in the range of $13.2 to $13.5 billion — a trajectory that, if sustained at the rates implied by the 2030 model, represents a compound annual revenue growth rate of roughly 13 to 15 percent from the fiscal 2025 base.

## The Tension the Reader Must Hold

Against that growth thesis sits a valuation and geopolitical risk set that this dossier treats with equal seriousness. KLA's enterprise value to trailing EBITDA multiple stood at approximately 29.7 times as of the frozen snapshot date, compared with a five-year median closer to 20 times — a premium that prices in substantial execution on the advanced-packaging ramp and the 2030 model with limited margin for cyclical slippage. Successive rounds of U.S. Department of Commerce export-control tightening compressed KLA's China revenue share from roughly 41 percent in fiscal 2024 to approximately 30 percent in fiscal 2025, with management guiding to an incremental $300 to $350 million revenue headwind in fiscal 2026 from the most recent control tranche alone.

| Metric | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026E |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total revenue (USD bn) | 9.81 | 12.16 | 13.2–13.5 |
| China revenue share | ~41% | ~30% | ~25–28% (est.) |
| Advanced packaging revenue | ~$500M | >$925M | >$1.0B |
| Services revenue | ~$2.1B | ~$2.5B | Growing |

The elevated multiple and China compression are not invalidations of the thesis; they are the conditions under which the thesis must be tested. Every subsequent chapter examines one dimension of that test.

chapters.title: From Photomask Inspector to Global Process Control Franchise: KLA's Five-Decade Accumulation
chapters.body:
## Physics as Business Model: The 1975 Founding

Kenneth Levy and Robert Anderson incorporated KLA Instruments Corporation in San Jose, California in 1975 with a proposition that has never fundamentally changed: semiconductor manufacturers lose far more money to undetected defects than they would spend on a tool capable of finding them. That asymmetry — the cost of a missed defect dwarfing the price of the inspection system — became the economic engine powering five decades of expansion.

The company's first commercially significant product crystallised the logic. Introduced in 1978, the RAPID photomask inspection system cut the time required to qualify a photomask from days to hours, eliminating a bottleneck that had grown more painful with every shrink in feature size. The tool did not merely speed up a manual process; it converted process uncertainty into a quantifiable yield number that a fab manager could act on. KLA went public in 1980, raising capital to pursue what its founders already understood to be a structurally growing market: as transistor geometries tightened, the consequences of an undetected contaminant or pattern deviation compounded, making inspection not a discretionary expenditure but an engineering necessity.

Two miles away in technology terms, though headquartered separately, Tencor Instruments was constructing a parallel franchise. Founded in 1976 by Karel Urbanek and John Schwabacher, Tencor approached the same yield-protection imperative from the surface side, developing laser-scanning technology for particle and contamination detection on unpatterned wafers and thin-film substrates. Through the 1980s, as the industry standardised on six-inch and then eight-inch wafers and as contamination control became a primary yield lever, Tencor's Surfscan family established a dominant position in unpatterned-wafer inspection and surface-characterisation metrology. The two companies were not competing — they were solving adjacent problems for the same customers.

## The 1997 Merger and the Architecture of Dominance

By the mid-1990s, the complementarity between KLA's patterned-wafer inspection franchise and Tencor's metrology and unpatterned-wafer leadership had become obvious to both management teams. In 1997 the two companies completed a $1.3 billion stock-for-stock transaction to form KLA-Tencor Corporation, combining what had been the strongest patterned-wafer inspection business with the strongest surface-characterisation and thin-film metrology platform. The merged entity held positions of market leadership across virtually every category of in-line process control equipment.

The industrial rationale was as important as the financial mechanics. Semiconductor fabs were transitioning through the 250-nanometre and 180-nanometre nodes, multi-layer metal interconnects were proliferating, and customers increasingly wanted a single process-control partner capable of monitoring every yield-critical step from incoming wafer through final patterned-layer inspection. The merged KLA-Tencor could offer that span in a way neither company could independently. Integration consumed several years of management attention, but the combined portfolio — inspection systems, overlay metrology, film-thickness measurement, reticle qualification tools — began generating cross-selling economics that standalone competitors could not replicate.

The post-merger decade saw KLA-Tencor deepen its position at the nodes where the industry's economics were concentrated. As leading-edge manufacturing migrated through 130 nanometres and into the 65-nanometre era, the number of patterning steps per wafer grew and the defect-budget per step shrank. KLA-Tencor's broadband-plasma optical inspection architecture, which illuminated wafer surfaces with a broad spectrum of wavelengths simultaneously rather than a single laser line, proved capable of capturing defect signatures that monochromatic systems missed. Market share in patterned-wafer inspection climbed toward 70 percent. The 2008 acquisitions of Therma-Wave — a specialist in thin-film characterisation and ion-implant metrology — and ICOS Vision Systems, a Belgian developer of back-end packaging inspection systems, extended the portfolio into optical metrology and die-level inspection respectively, signalling that KLA-Tencor's ambitions reached beyond the traditional front-end wafer process.

## The Wallace Era: Services as Strategic Architecture

Rick Wallace became Chief Executive Officer in January 2006, having joined KLA in 1988 as an applications engineer and worked through product line management, marketing, and business development. His institutional knowledge of the company's physics stack was matched by an increasingly clear-eyed view of its financial vulnerabilities. Semiconductor equipment spending is cyclical; fab customers defer capital programmes during downturns, and a company whose revenue is predominantly tied to new tool shipments will see earnings compress sharply in down years regardless of the quality of its technology.

Wallace's strategic response, crystallised in the 2012–2016 period, was to deepen the services and software monetisation layer sitting on top of KLA-Tencor's installed base of tens of thousands of tools deployed in fabs worldwide. The installed base was already generating substantial spare-parts and maintenance revenue, but the company had not fully exploited the data flowing from those tools. The introduction of subscription-based process-control software — Klarity and the Design2Yield platform — changed the architecture of the customer relationship. Rather than selling a tool and waiting for the next capital cycle, KLA-Tencor was now selling ongoing analytical capability: algorithms that ingested defect-signature data from across a customer's installed fleet, identified correlating defect patterns across process steps, and surfaced actionable yield-improvement recommendations.

The services revenue compounding that began in this period has never stopped. By fiscal 2025, KLA Global Services had posted year-over-year revenue growth for fifty consecutive quarters, a streak spanning the 2015–2016 memory downturn, the 2018–2019 trade-war disruption, the 2020 pandemic, and the 2023 memory trough. Annual services revenue reached approximately $2.5 billion in fiscal 2025, representing roughly 22 percent of total revenue, and carrying structural margins that exceed equipment margins. The financial architecture Wallace constructed — a high-margin, recurring services base that sustains the income statement through equipment-cycle troughs — is perhaps his most durable strategic contribution.

## Orbotech and the Expansion Beyond the Wafer

The acquisition of Orbotech Ltd., which closed in February 2019 for $3.4 billion, was the most transformative deal since the 1997 merger. Orbotech was an Israeli-headquartered technology company with dominant positions in printed-circuit-board inspection, flat-panel-display manufacturing equipment, and — crucially — advanced-packaging process tools. Its inspection, direct-imaging, and optical-shaping systems were deployed in virtually every significant PCB and display manufacturer globally.

The strategic rationale extended beyond revenue diversification. Orbotech's engineering base in Migdal HaEmek, Israel, brought optical and imaging expertise that reinforced KLA's core detection physics. More importantly, the advanced-packaging equipment Orbotech had developed for substrate and IC-package manufacturers aligned precisely with a structural shift that the semiconductor industry was beginning to make: as transistor scaling slowed at advanced nodes, performance gains increasingly required tighter integration at the package level — chiplets, heterogeneous integration, high-bandwidth memory stacks. The inspection and metrology requirements for these architectures were approaching the complexity of front-end wafer processes, and KLA needed a position in that market before its customers committed to other platforms.

In July 2019, the company renamed itself KLA Corporation, dropping "Tencor" from the identity it had carried for twenty-two years. The rename was not cosmetic. It signalled that the company's remit now spanned the full electronics value chain — from silicon wafer through front-end patterned-wafer process to PCB substrate and advanced package — and that the Tencor lineage, while honoured, no longer defined the boundaries of the business.

## The AI Inflection and the 2030 Target

The demand environment that KLA Corporation entered in fiscal 2023 and 2024 was structurally different from any it had navigated before. The acceleration of AI infrastructure investment by the hyperscale cloud providers and their semiconductor supply chains generated inspection requirements at every level of the stack: gate-all-around nanosheet transistors at two-nanometre and below at TSMC and Samsung Foundry, high-bandwidth memory stacks at SK Hynix and Micron requiring sub-micron bonding-alignment control, and chiplet assemblies on advanced substrates demanding die-placement and interconnect inspection that the back-end market had not historically required.

KLA's CIRCL-AP platform and related advanced-packaging tools moved from a nascent revenue line to a material business with speed that surprised even the company's own guidance. Advanced-packaging revenues exceeded $925 million in fiscal 2025, up approximately 85 percent year over year from roughly $500 million in fiscal 2024 — a category that had barely registered on the revenue line in fiscal 2022. The trajectory prompted management to raise advanced-packaging guidance twice within a single fiscal year.

The China export-control compression — KLA's China revenue share contracted from approximately 41 percent in fiscal 2024 to roughly 30 percent in fiscal 2025 following successive rounds of U.S. Department of Commerce restrictions — created a real headwind, with management guiding to an incremental $300–$350 million revenue impact in fiscal 2026. But the structural demand from Taiwan, Korea, and the United States more than offset the China contraction in aggregate.

On March 12, 2026, Wallace presented the company's 2030 target model to investors: $26 billion in revenue, approximately 63.5 percent gross margin, 45–47 percent operating margin, and $84 in non-GAAP diluted earnings per share. The board simultaneously authorised a $7.0 billion supplemental share-repurchase programme and approved a 21 percent increase in the quarterly dividend.

> "KLA is a key enabler of the AI ecosystem," Wallace told investors in the quarters leading to that presentation — a formulation that captured both the demand dynamic and the company's own understanding of where it sits in the technology supply chain.

The five-decade accumulation that began with a photomask inspector in 1978 had produced, by the spring of 2026, a $140-billion-market-capitalisation process-control franchise with near-monopoly positions in patterned-wafer inspection and broad leadership across the inspection and metrology market — sustained by an installed base whose data advantages compound with every additional tool shipped and every additional quarter of Klarity subscriptions renewed.

chapters.title: The Physics-Intensive Portfolio: Inspection Systems, Metrology Platforms, and the Advanced Packaging Suite
chapters.body:
## A Portfolio Built on Physics

KLA Corporation's product architecture reflects a deliberate strategic axiom: that the most defensible position in the semiconductor supply chain belongs not to the company that builds the transistor, but to the one that determines whether it was built correctly. Across three reporting segments — Semiconductor Process Control at roughly 91 percent of fiscal 2025 revenues, Specialty Semiconductor Process at approximately 4 percent, and PCB and Component Inspection at the remaining 5 percent — KLA has assembled an interlocking suite of physics-intensive measurement and inspection systems that no competitor has fully replicated in any single category, let alone across all of them.

The portfolio logic is cumulative. Each tool generates data. Data improves recipes. Better recipes justify premium pricing on subsequent tool generations. The loop has been running since the RAPID photomask inspection system shipped in 1978, and its compounding effect is visible in gross margins that have expanded from the mid-50s to a sustained 61–62 percent range over the past half-decade.

## Semiconductor Process Control: Detection at the Limits of Physics

The core of Semiconductor Process Control is patterned-wafer inspection — finding killer defects on in-process silicon before they propagate through additional lithography and deposition steps that each add cost. KLA's dominant platform here is the Broadband Plasma series, currently spanning the 29xx and 39xx families. BBP inspection illuminates the wafer surface with a broadband light source — covering a wide spectral range from deep ultraviolet into the visible — and captures scattered, reflected, and diffracted light across multiple collection angles simultaneously. The multi-spectral architecture enables the tool to distinguish true defects from process noise even on the near-periodic structures produced by extreme-ultraviolet lithography, where a single stochastic printing error can kill dozens of transistors on a gate-all-around nanosheet device. The sensitivity required at N2 and below — sub-nanometre height variations, particles well under 20 nanometres — demands light-source stability, optical-train alignment tolerances, and signal-processing fidelity that took KLA more than a decade to achieve at volume. Applied Materials and Onto Innovation have published competing approaches; neither has displaced the BBP as the specified inspection platform at TSMC or Samsung Foundry for leading-edge patterned layers.

Where optical wavelengths physically cannot resolve, electron-beam inspection takes over. KLA's e-beam tools scan the wafer with a focused electron beam, detecting electrical and structural anomalies at sub-10-nanometre scales that a photon-based system cannot see. Throughput is an order of magnitude lower than optical tools, making e-beam a complementary rather than replacement technology — deployed at the most critical layers where defect density must be driven to near-zero and where the cost of a missed defect is highest. The tool's role is growing as logic nodes compress and multi-patterning sequences multiply the opportunity for overlay-induced bridging defects that are electrically latent and invisible to optical inspection at standard sensitivity.

Unpatterned-wafer inspection — the legacy of the Tencor Instruments merger — is handled by the Surfscan family, which uses laser-scattering technology to detect particles, surface roughness anomalies, and crystal-originated pits on polished silicon and epitaxial substrates before any device structures are formed. Silicon wafer manufacturers and IDMs running epitaxial substrate qualification are the primary customers. The physics is different from patterned inspection: without device structures to mask the signal, the tool can use oblique-angle dark-field illumination to achieve particle-detection sensitivities below 20 nanometres on a 300-millimetre substrate, and the absence of pattern-induced noise makes the statistical problem tractable even at high scan speeds.

Reticle inspection — protecting the photomasks that define the circuit pattern at every lithography step — is served by the Teron and STARlight platforms. A reticle is used thousands of times in a fab; a single print defect on the mask propagates to every wafer printed with it. The Teron series uses transmitted-light and reflected-light imaging at multiple wavelengths; the STARlight systems, designed for EUV reticle inspection, must detect sub-resolution assist features and phase-defect variations on a mask that costs upward of $300,000 to manufacture. KLA holds a near-exclusive position in reticle inspection: the physics of EUV actinic inspection has proven difficult enough that ASML's own EUV-wavelength mask inspection programme has moved slowly, leaving KLA's non-actinic platforms as the practical standard in high-volume manufacturing.

On the metrology side, the Archer platform dominates overlay measurement — quantifying the alignment between successive patterned layers with sub-angstrom precision. As EUV and multi-patterning produce structures where misalignment of even 0.5 nanometres can flip a device from functional to broken, overlay metrology has grown from a process-monitoring function into a process-control loop running at every critical layer. The Spectra and SpectraShape families address optical critical dimension measurement — using spectroscopic scatterometry to infer the three-dimensional shape of sub-resolution features from the way they diffract broadband light. SpectraFilm extends the capability to thin-film stack characterisation, measuring thickness, composition, and stress in dielectric and metal layers. These are not interchangeable with atomic force microscopes or cross-sectional transmission electron microscopy: they are in-line, high-throughput, non-destructive platforms that a fab can run on every wafer, not as a once-per-lot sample.

## Advanced Packaging: A Different Physics Problem

The advanced-packaging segment has emerged as KLA's fastest-growing revenue category precisely because hybrid bonding and chiplet integration present a detection challenge that front-end wafer inspection tools were not designed to solve. Front-end inspection assumes planar silicon with periodic structures and film thicknesses measured in nanometres to tens of nanometres. Hybrid bonding — the direct copper-to-copper interconnect that enables HBM memory stacks and logic-on-logic chiplet integration at pitches of 1 to 3 microns — presents a surface that is partially bonded, thermally stressed, and geometrically variable in ways that frustrate the pattern-recognition algorithms and illumination geometries optimised for leading-edge logic wafers.

KLA's CIRCL-AP platform was engineered specifically for panel-level and die-level advanced-packaging inspection. The system handles the larger substrates and non-standard geometries of advanced-packaging flows — fan-out wafer-level packaging, embedded die, and reconstituted wafer formats that can reach panel dimensions of 600 by 600 millimetres — while maintaining the defect-sensitivity required to catch misaligned copper pillars, delamination at the bond interface, or void formation in the hybrid-bond layer that would cause an open circuit in a stack that may contain 32 DRAM dies. The KT Aligner platform addresses die-placement inspection after dicing, verifying that chiplets are positioned within the placement tolerances required for a heterogeneous integration flow to achieve its interconnect density targets.

Revenue attributed to advanced packaging exceeded $925 million in fiscal 2025, up approximately 85 percent year over year, driven by HBM3E and HBM4 production ramps at SK Hynix, Samsung Semiconductor, and Micron Technology, and by CoWoS advanced-packaging qualification at TSMC for AI-accelerator customers including NVIDIA and Broadcom. The $925 million figure represents a category that was barely a line item in KLA's fiscal 2022 annual report; management's trajectory toward $2 billion-plus by the end of the decade is grounded in the observable physics constraint that hybrid-bonding pitch reduction from the current 3-micron generation toward sub-1-micron cannot proceed without correspondingly tighter process control.

## Specialty Semiconductor Process: The Atomic-Layer Adjacency

The Specialty Semiconductor Process segment — roughly $500 million in annual revenue — contributes KLA's etch and deposition capabilities for applications that fall outside the leading-edge logic and memory flows. The segment's atomic-layer-etch and atomic-layer-deposition tools serve MEMS device manufacturers, LED and micro-LED producers, SiC and GaN power-device fabs, and advanced-packaging substrate processors. KLA entered atomic-layer processing rather than licensing the technology because the integration of process tools with process-control metrology creates a closed-loop capability that neither a standalone ALE vendor nor a standalone metrology vendor can replicate. When a SiC etch step runs on a KLA platform, the tool's sensor suite measures the etch depth and uniformity in real time, and that data feeds back into the next wafer's process recipe without a separate metrology pass. The strategic logic is adjacency to the inspection franchise: SSP tools create the kind of installed-base data relationships that generate service revenue and software-subscription revenue on the same compounding loop as the core SPC business.

## PCB and Component Inspection: The Orbotech Heritage and the AI Substrate Revival

The PCB and Component Inspection segment — approximately $600 million in fiscal 2025 revenues — represents the Orbotech legacy acquired in the $3.4 billion transaction that closed in February 2019. The segment provides direct imaging systems that expose PCB and IC-substrate circuit patterns using laser or LED illumination in place of photomasks, optical inspection systems for finished boards and IC substrates, optical shaping and surface-modification tools, inkjet printing for solder-mask and functional-fluid deposition, and CAM/CAE software for design-to-manufacture translation.

The segment's strategic relevance is being redefined by AI infrastructure. Advanced IC substrates — the organic interposers that connect logic and memory dies in 2.5D configurations — require line-and-space geometries that are shrinking toward 2/2-micron routing, redistribution-layer pitches that approach advanced-packaging tolerances, and inspection regimes that match the defect density requirements of a substrate supporting a $10,000 GPU. KLA's direct-imaging and inspection platforms are specified at substrate suppliers serving NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel Foundry customers; the segment's revenue growth has outpaced the broader PCB market as AI server bills of materials shift toward high-density interconnect substrates at volumes and unit values that were not contemplated when the Orbotech deal was struck.

## The Software Moat: Klarity and the Proprietary Defect Database

Underneath every hardware platform sits the data-intelligence layer that converts KLA's installed base of tens of thousands of tools into a compounding algorithmic moat. Klarity — the flagship process-runtime software suite — aggregates defect-signature data from inspection tools at customer fabs globally, building a continuously updated library of defect classifications, tool-to-tool matching algorithms, and process-control recipes that any single customer's data would be insufficient to generate.

The Design2Yield platform connects defect-inspection data to circuit-design databases, enabling semiconductor engineers to identify which layout patterns are systematically producing failures and to feed that information back into the design rules that govern the next chip revision. KLAROS provides a unified factory-data platform linking KLA tool outputs to the fab's process information management system, closing the loop between in-line measurement and process adjustment. Together these platforms generate subscription revenue with structurally higher margins than hardware, are embedded in the fab's process-qualification documentation, and cannot be switched out without requalifying the entire inspection and metrology flow — a twelve-to-eighteen-month undertaking that no logic fab on a node-transition timeline is willing to contemplate.

No competitor has replicated the Klarity defect database at KLA's scale. Building it would require an installed base large enough to observe the full statistical distribution of defect types across every process integration scheme in volume production — a base that took KLA five decades to accumulate and that requires market share approaching monopoly to maintain. Hardware cycles end; the recipe database compounds indefinitely.

## A Revenue Trajectory Reshaped by Structure, Not Cycle

Six fiscal years of KLA's income statement compress a story of structural expansion punctuated by one inventory-correction trough. Revenue climbed from approximately $6.9 billion in fiscal 2021 to $12.16 billion in fiscal 2025 — a 76 percent expansion in four years — before entering fiscal 2026 on a quarterly run rate pointing toward a full-year total near $13.3 billion. The compound growth rate across that span exceeded 12 percent annually, faster than global wafer-fabrication equipment spending as a whole, reflecting KLA's rising revenue per wafer pass as nodes advance and its structurally expanding addressable market in advanced packaging.

The fiscal 2024 dip to $9.81 billion from fiscal 2023's approximate $10.5 billion peak reflected the post-2022 memory-inventory correction. DRAM and NAND customers deferred equipment purchases while working down elevated channel inventory, and that softness propagated into inspection-tool spending even though process-control deferral carries higher long-run yield cost than deferrals in etch or deposition. Recovery was correspondingly sharp. [Fiscal 2025 revenue of $12.16 billion](https://ir.kla.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/500/kla-corporation-reports-fiscal-2025-fourth-quarter-and-full) represented 23.9 percent year-over-year growth, with weakness in China — whose revenue share contracted from approximately 41 percent to 30 percent — replaced by simultaneous strength in Taiwan, Korea, and the United States. Fiscal 2026 has continued the acceleration: quarterly revenues of $3.21 billion (Q1), [$3.297 billion](https://ir.kla.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/509/kla-corporation-reports-fiscal-2026-second-quarter-results) (Q2, described at the time as a record), and $3.415 billion (Q3) implied a full fiscal year at the high end of management's $13.2–$13.5 billion range.

| Non-GAAP Net Income ($B) | ~2.4 | ~3.6 | ~3.9 | ~3.8 | ~4.5 | ~5.0 |
| GAAP Diluted EPS | ~$14 | ~$23 | ~$25 | ~$25 | $30.37 | ~$37 |
| Non-GAAP Diluted EPS | ~$17 | ~$25 | ~$27 | ~$27 | ~$34 | ~$36–38 |
| Free Cash Flow ($B) | ~2.2 | ~3.2 | ~3.5 | ~3.5 | ~4.4 | ~5.0 |

*FY2021–FY2023 approximate; FY2024–FY2025 from audited results; FY2026E sums Q1–Q3 actuals plus Q4 guidance midpoint of $3.35 billion. Fiscal year ends June 30.*

## The Gross Margin Inflection: From Mid-50s to 62 Percent

The most consequential structural shift in KLA's income statement over the past decade is not revenue scale but margin transformation. Gross margins expanded from the 55–57 percent range prevalent across 2018–2020 to a sustained 61–62 percent across fiscal 2024–2026 — a 400–700 basis-point improvement sustained through equipment cycles in which component-cost inflation and supply-chain complexity were persistent headwinds for the sector. The expansion was not a single-event step change but the compounding of four distinct structural forces.

The first and most durable driver has been services mix enrichment. The KLA Global Services organisation — comprising spare parts, extended warranties, time-and-materials contracts, and Klarity software subscriptions — contributed approximately $2.5 billion in fiscal 2025, representing roughly 22 percent of total revenue and its [fiftieth consecutive quarter](https://ir.kla.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/500/kla-corporation-reports-fiscal-2025-fourth-quarter-and-full) of year-over-year growth. Services carry structurally higher gross margins than equipment because incremental contract revenue flows against a largely fixed field-service and remote-diagnostics cost base. As the installed base of KLA tools has grown to tens of thousands of systems globally, the services revenue annuity has compounded without proportional increases in cost of goods sold.

The second driver is Klarity software licence revenue. Klarity, KLA's factory-wide process-control intelligence platform, transitioned from a bundled software feature to a standalone subscription offering through the 2018–2022 period. Software licences carry near-100 percent incremental gross margins; their growing contribution to the services revenue mix has diluted the cost-of-goods-sold denominator disproportionately. Management has declined to quantify Klarity's standalone revenue contribution, but the trajectory of aggregate services margins relative to equipment margins provides a structural signal.

Third, pricing power on advanced-node tool generations has allowed KLA to recover component-cost inflation while simultaneously expanding gross dollars per unit. Broadband-plasma inspection systems deployed at N3 and N2 logic nodes command substantially higher average selling prices than their N7 and N5 predecessors, reflecting the greater detection-sensitivity requirements — and correspondingly higher customer value per avoided defect — at each advancing node. KLA's near-monopoly in patterned-wafer inspection, with an estimated 75–80 percent market share, eliminates the competitive pricing pressure that would otherwise suppress tool-generation step-ups.

Fourth, reduced warranty accruals on mature platform generations have lowered cost of goods sold modestly. As tools enter their third and fourth production years, manufacturing defect rates decline and warranty reserve releases improve reported gross margin. Several tool families introduced in 2019–2021 entered this mature-accrual phase during fiscal 2024–2025. The 2030 target gross margin of approximately 63.5 percent — presented at the March 2026 Investor Day — implies incremental expansion of 150–200 basis points from the fiscal 2025–2026 run rate, achievable through continued services mix shift and Klarity subscription penetration rather than through a step-change in equipment margins.

## China Compression: Quantifying the Headwind

No single external variable more precisely tested KLA's structural earnings resilience over the past two fiscal years than successive rounds of U.S. Department of Commerce export-control tightening targeting China's advanced semiconductor ecosystem. The arithmetic is stark. In fiscal 2024, China represented approximately 41 percent of total revenues — approximately $4.0 billion on a $9.81 billion base. By fiscal 2025, China's share had contracted to roughly 30 percent, translating to approximately $3.65 billion on a $12.16 billion base. In absolute terms, China revenue declined by approximately $370 million even as total company revenue grew $2.35 billion. The rest of the world, in other words, delivered approximately $2.72 billion of incremental revenue — a feat obscured by the headline growth rate and illustrating the degree to which foundry/logic demand in Taiwan, Korea, and the United States filled the geographic void.

Management guided at the December 2024 investor call to an incremental $300–$350 million revenue headwind attributable to the most recent control tranche in fiscal 2026. Against a $13.3 billion base, that headwind represents approximately 2.4 percent of revenue — material but absorbable given the pace of demand recovery at TSMC's expanding Taiwan and Arizona facilities, Samsung Foundry, and Intel Foundry Services. By the midpoint of fiscal 2026, China's share was tracking toward approximately 25–27 percent of total revenues, a structurally lower plateau absent policy reversal.

The margin implications of a hypothetical further restriction scenario warrant explicit modelling. At KLA's gross margin of approximately 62 percent, each $1 billion of China revenue carries roughly $620 million of gross profit. A scenario in which China revenue fell from 30 percent to 15 percent of an otherwise-unchanged $13.3 billion base would eliminate approximately $2.0 billion of revenue and roughly $1.24 billion of gross profit — a 17 percent gross-profit reduction before any operating-cost adjustment. The primary offset mechanism is geographic substitution: because KLA's advanced-node inspection monopoly means the underlying wafer-start growth that China was serving cannot be served by any alternative supplier, that production shifts to other geographies where KLA tools are already specified. The net revenue loss from a hypothetical China withdrawal to 15 percent would be substantially smaller than the gross China revenue reduction, though the speed of geographic capacity ramp determines the timing of offset.

## Capital Structure: Permanent Leverage, Compounding Returns

KLA's capital structure reflects a management philosophy that treats long-term debt not as a deleveraging target but as permanently efficient balance-sheet engineering. Approximately $6.5–7 billion in long-term debt, rated investment-grade, services at rates well below the company's return on invested capital, making paydown a capital-allocation error relative to the alternatives. Annual R&D investment of approximately $900 million–$1.2 billion — roughly 10–12 percent of revenue at the fiscal 2025 scale — ensures that the tool portfolio remains ahead of next-generation detection-sensitivity requirements, protecting the inspection monopoly against the physics-barrier challenge of each successive node transition.

With those two capital claims settled, free cash flow has flowed almost entirely to shareholders. Fiscal 2025 free cash flow of approximately $4.4 billion supported a capital-return programme that has compounded per-share equity value for over a decade. At the March 2026 Investor Day, the board authorised a [$7.0 billion supplemental share-repurchase programme](https://ir.kla.com/financial-information/financial-results) — the largest in the company's history — and raised the quarterly dividend 21 percent to $2.30 per share, up from $1.90.

The cash arithmetic is instructive. At approximately 133.7 million diluted shares outstanding — implied by fiscal 2025 GAAP net income of $4.06 billion divided by diluted EPS of $30.37 — the $2.30 quarterly dividend implies an annual outlay of approximately $1.23 billion. With free cash flow approaching $5 billion annually in fiscal 2026, the dividend consumes roughly 25 cents of every free-cash-flow dollar, leaving approximately $3.75 billion available for buybacks and balance-sheet management. If deployed against the share price implied by the pre-split trading level of approximately $2,059 (a 10-for-1 split was effective June 2026), the $7.0 billion authorisation represents approximately one-fifth of the company's market capitalisation — an aggressive EPS accretion lever that at fiscal 2025's $30.37 GAAP EPS base could add $4–6 per share annually as the float contracts.

## Backlog: Lead-Time Normalisation, Not Demand Softness

KLA's order backlog stood at $7.86 billion at June 30, 2025, down from $9.83 billion a year earlier — a $1.97 billion decline that, read superficially, suggests order-rate deterioration. The contextual interpretation is almost the opposite. During 2021–2023, semiconductor-equipment lead times extended dramatically as supply-chain congestion, component shortages, and customer pull-forward ordering inflated backlog to artificial peaks. The subsequent normalisation — as supply chains cleared and lead times compressed from 18-plus months toward 9–12 months at many tool categories — mechanically reduced backlog without any change in underlying end-market demand.

[Management estimated](https://ir.kla.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/500/kla-corporation-reports-fiscal-2025-fourth-quarter-and-full) that 71–76 percent of the June 2025 backlog would be recognised as revenue within 12 months and 20–25 percent in the following 12 months. That conversion cadence implied approximately $5.6–6.0 billion of backlog-derived revenue in fiscal 2026, covering the majority of the guided annual total without relying on new orders booked in the year. The remaining revenue requirement was largely services renewals and spare-parts demand carrying minimal cancellation risk — a structure that gives KLA roughly 18–24 months of forward revenue visibility and underpins the narrow analyst consensus bands around its quarterly guidance.

## The 2030 Model Bridge: Compounding to $26 Billion

The revenue model presented at the March 2026 Investor Day calls for $26 billion in fiscal 2030 revenue, approximately 63.5 percent gross margin, 45–47 percent operating margin, and $84 in non-GAAP diluted EPS. From a fiscal 2025 base of $12.16 billion, reaching $26 billion by fiscal 2030 requires a compound annual growth rate of approximately 13–15 percent — ambitious by capital-equipment industry standards but consistent with the demand environment KLA was describing to its institutional shareholders.

Three revenue pillars support the bridge. Leading-edge wafer-starts growth — driven by gate-all-around nanosheet transitions at 2-nanometre and below at TSMC, Samsung Foundry, and Intel Foundry — raises KLA's revenue per wafer pass as each multi-patterning step requires a dedicated inspection tool. Management has characterised a 2-nanometre wafer as generating roughly 35–40 percent more inspection-tool revenue per pass than a 5-nanometre wafer, meaning node mix shift toward leading-edge compounds revenue independent of unit wafer-volume growth.

Advanced packaging constitutes the second pillar. Revenue from hybrid-bonding, HBM inspection, and chiplet-assembly metrology exceeded $925 million in fiscal 2025 — a category that barely appeared on KLA's revenue line three fiscal years earlier. The trajectory toward $2 billion or more in advanced-packaging revenue by fiscal 2030 is anchored by HBM4 production ramps required for next-generation AI accelerators, the proliferation of chiplet architectures across every major semiconductor company, and the extension of hybrid-bonding pitch tolerances that demand inspection tool sensitivity beyond what legacy back-end equipment can provide.

Services compounding provides the third and most durable pillar. As the installed base expands with each year of equipment shipments, the services annuity grows proportionally, with no customer-acquisition cost. At the fiscal 2025 ratio of approximately $2.5 billion in services against an installed base of tens of thousands of tools, even conservative assumptions around installed-base growth and Klarity subscription penetration support services revenue of $4 billion or more by fiscal 2030.

The operating-leverage mechanics that drive margin expansion from approximately 42–44 percent (fiscal 2025–2026) to 45–47 percent (fiscal 2030) are primarily gross-margin-driven: the mix shift toward software and services — both at structurally higher gross margins than equipment — pulls the blended margin higher, while operating-expense growth is constrained by KLA's policy of managing headcount additions against revenue scale. R&D spending, while growing in absolute dollars, has tracked below the revenue growth rate in recent years, producing positive operating leverage without sacrificing the physics-intensive research that sustains the inspection monopoly at each successive node.

> "KLA is a key enabler of the AI ecosystem," CEO Rick Wallace told analysts following the record second-quarter fiscal 2026 result. The statement was not marketing language. Every gate-all-around transistor, every HBM stack, every chiplet-bonding interface processed at the leading edge depends on inspection and metrology tools that KLA, in several critical categories, remains the only supplier capable of delivering at production scale.

chapters.title: What the Market Is Pricing In: Multiple Anatomy, Peer Comparison, and Bull/Base/Bear Scenarios
chapters.body:
## A Premium That Demands Justification

At approximately $2,059 per share on the frozen-window date of May 23, 2026, KLA Corporation traded at a trailing GAAP price-to-earnings multiple of roughly 60 times. The non-GAAP lens is gentler but not comforting: full-year fiscal 2026 non-GAAP EPS consensus centred on $36 to $38, placing the forward non-GAAP P/E at 55 to 57 times. On an enterprise-value basis, applying the approximately $263 billion market capitalisation and roughly $6.5 billion of long-term debt against trailing twelve-month EBITDA of approximately $9.1 billion produces an EV/EBITDA of 29.7 times — a multiple last sustained at semiconductor-equipment companies during the peak of the 2021 cycle. EV/Sales runs 20 to 21 times on the same basis, and price-to-free-cash-flow — using the $4.4 billion fiscal 2025 figure trending toward $5 billion in fiscal 2026 — sits at approximately 53 to 58 times. Price-to-book is largely uninstructive given the buyback-compressed equity base but stands near 20 times.

The summary question embedded in those multiples: is KLA a cyclical equipment company that happens to sit near the top of a spending wave, or a compounding franchise whose inspection-and-metrology moat constitutes a durable, growing earnings stream? The current price answers emphatically: the latter. Whether that answer remains correct is the central valuation question.

## Peer-Group Multiples: Premium Anatomy

A direct peer comparison contextualises the absolute figures.

| Company | Trailing P/E | Forward P/E | EV/EBITDA | EV/Sales | Gross Margin | 5-yr Rev. CAGR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| KLA (KLAC) | ~60x | ~55–57x | ~29.7x | ~20–21x | 61–62% | ~21% |
| Applied Materials (AMAT) | ~22x | ~19x | ~20x | ~6x | ~48% | ~14% |
| Lam Research (LRCX) | ~26x | ~22x | ~25x | ~9x | ~47% | ~13% |
| Onto Innovation (ONTO) | ~35x | ~28x | ~22x | ~8x | ~50% | ~18% |
| ASML (ASML) | ~38x | ~32x | ~34x | ~14x | ~51% | ~16% |

*Multiples as of May 2026 frozen-window snapshot; forward P/E based on next-twelve-month consensus estimates.*

The premium KLA commands over Applied Materials and Lam Research — the two largest equipment peers by revenue — is substantial and persistent. Applied Materials, with revenues roughly twice KLA's and comparable AI-infrastructure exposure, trades at 20x EV/EBITDA. The delta to KLA's 29.7x reflects three structural differentials: gross margins running 13 to 14 percentage points above AMAT's (a product of the inspection-and-metrology market structure, where KLA has no direct substitute at the patterned-wafer bright-field inspection step); a services mix at 22 percent of revenues and rising, which elevates blended margins; and a five-year revenue CAGR of roughly 21 percent against AMAT's 14 percent. Lam Research's 25x EV/EBITDA trades closer to KLA but reflects heavier exposure to DRAM and NAND etch cycles, which are more violent than foundry/logic. The Lam discount is a memory-cycle discount.

Onto Innovation, the most direct small-cap competitor in advanced-packaging metrology and the one peer gaining qualification slots at AI-accelerator customers, trades at 22x EV/EBITDA — a meaningful discount that reflects execution uncertainty at scale and an installed base that remains a fraction of KLA's. ASML, at 34x EV/EBITDA, is the only peer commanding a higher multiple, justified by its outright monopoly on extreme-ultraviolet lithography systems and a per-unit ASP exceeding $180 million for high-NA tools. KLA's discount to ASML is rational: lithography absorbs a larger share of leading-edge fab capex than process control, concentrating pricing power even further.

## Historical Multiple Regimes and Cycle Positioning

KLA's EV/EBITDA has traversed a wide range across spending cycles. During the trough of the 2022 downturn — when memory customers halted equipment purchases and KLA's fiscal 2024 revenues declined approximately 7 percent year-over-year — the multiple compressed to roughly 12 times. The five-year median has settled near 20 times, reflecting the market's central estimate of a business that grows through cycles but is not immune to them.

The current 29.7 times is roughly 50 percent above that median — a premium historically durable only when: accelerating revenue growth pushes forward earnings estimates higher faster than the stock price, effectively normalising the multiple in real time; a structural demand shift persuades the market to permanently re-rate the earnings stream; and no visible catalyst for a cycle reversal has emerged. All three conditions are, as of May 2026, nominally in place. Revenue grew 24 percent in fiscal 2025 and is tracking 9 to 11 percent growth in fiscal 2026. Management has articulated a structural AI demand narrative. And while export-control headwinds and a latent memory cycle risk are visible, neither has yet registered as a revenue inflection. The risk is that multiple expansion of this magnitude has historically reversed sharply once any condition breaks: in 2022, the multiple fell from approximately 28 to 30 times to 12 times in fewer than eighteen months.

## Reverse-DCF: What Is Priced In

At a midpoint enterprise value of approximately $263 billion, a simple reverse-DCF exercise is revealing. Assuming a 9 percent weighted-average cost of capital, a 3.5 percent terminal growth rate, and a 35 percent terminal FCF margin on revenues, the implied year-ten revenue — working backwards from the current EV — is approximately $33 to $36 billion, with FCF of $11.5 to $12.5 billion.

Management's 2030 target model calls for $26 billion in revenue and approximately $84 non-GAAP EPS. At a normalised 30 to 32 percent FCF-to-revenue conversion on that base, 2030 FCF would be approximately $7.8 to $8.3 billion. The market is therefore not merely pricing in the 2030 model — it is pricing in the 2030 model plus continued compounding thereafter, with limited multiple normalisation. Consensus estimates for fiscal 2028 revenue cluster around $19 to $21 billion; the current multiple is consistent with those estimates only if the terminal multiple three years forward remains at 24 times or above. That is not a mean-reversion scenario. It is a sustained-premium scenario — the bet made on ASML from 2015 through 2023, which proved correct, and the bet the market is now making on KLA.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — implied pre-split price: approximately $3,200–$3,500.** AI infrastructure capital expenditure accelerates into fiscal 2028, advanced-packaging revenues hit $2 billion by fiscal 2028 — roughly two years ahead of the implicit 2030 trajectory — driven by HBM4 and hybrid-bonding proliferation at TSMC and Samsung, and China restrictions remain static. The 2030 model is achieved in fiscal 2029. FY2030 EBITDA of approximately $12 billion (on $26 billion revenue at a 46 percent margin) at a 32x multiple yields enterprise value of roughly $384 billion. Less $6.5 billion of structural debt and divided by approximately 112 million shares after continued buybacks, the implied pre-split price is approximately $3,370 — roughly 64 percent upside from May 2026 levels.

**Base case — implied pre-split price: approximately $2,400–$2,600.** The 2030 model is achieved on schedule. Revenue compounds at roughly 13 percent annually. The multiple normalises toward 24 to 26 times EV/EBITDA as the cycle matures. FY2030 EBITDA of approximately $11.7 billion at 25x yields enterprise value of $293 billion; equity value after debt of approximately $286 billion divided by roughly 115 million shares gives a pre-split price near $2,487 — approximately 21 percent upside over four years, implying mid-single-digit total-return per annum before dividends.

**Bear case — implied pre-split price: approximately $950–$1,100.** A semiconductor-equipment down-cycle begins in fiscal 2027 — plausible if AI infrastructure spending plateaus as hyperscalers absorb recent chip purchases or if GPU-generation timing slips. Export controls tighten further, compressing China revenues from 30 percent to 15 percent of the total. Advanced-packaging ramps more slowly than guided. Revenue stalls near $16 to $18 billion. At a trough multiple of 19 times on compressed EBITDA of approximately $6.5 billion, enterprise value falls to roughly $124 billion; equity value of approximately $117 billion divided by approximately 125 million shares (buybacks slow in a downturn) implies a pre-split price near $936 — a 55 percent decline from current levels, consistent with KLA's 2022 drawdown experience.

## The Stock Split: Accessibility, Not Alchemy

The 10-for-1 forward split announced in May 2026 and effective June 12, 2026 — converting each $2,059 share into ten shares at approximately $206 — carries a well-worn debate: do splits create value? The evidence from comparable technology-sector events is directionally positive but modest. NVIDIA's July 2021 4-for-1 split preceded continued appreciation as retail participation increased and index-rebalancing flows amplified demand; Amazon's June 2022 20-for-1 split coincided with prolonged multiple compression driven by macro forces unrelated to the split itself. The academic consensus holds that splits are value-neutral in frictionless markets — they alter neither the earnings stream nor the capital structure.

In practice the effect is real but small: lower per-share prices increase retail accessibility, reduce bid-ask spread as a percentage of price, and widen the options market by enabling standard strike increments at the $206 post-split level. For KLA, whose pre-split price effectively excluded most retail-scale option strategies and some institutional mandates with per-share-price constraints, the split addresses a genuine accessibility issue. What it does not address is the valuation. At 29.7 times EV/EBITDA, the market has already embedded a great deal of optimism into KLA's price. The split changes the denominator of the per-share figure; only execution on the 2030 model — $26 billion in revenue, $84 in non-GAAP EPS, advanced-packaging revenues compounding through the chiplet era — will change the numerator.

chapters.title: The Quarterly Cadence: Revenue Beats, Management Commentary, and the AI Demand Signal
chapters.body:
The eleven quarterly earnings periods KLA traversed between the first quarter of fiscal 2024 and the third quarter of fiscal 2026 drew an almost unbroken ascending line through a cycle that, in prior semiconductor-equipment expansions, would have produced at least one material correction. It did not. Instead, the period traced a base-to-inflection arc: a cyclically softened fiscal 2024, a decisive 23.9 percent revenue step in fiscal 2025, and a sequential-record sequence in fiscal 2026 that carried management's language from measured optimism to explicit identification of KLA as a structural beneficiary of the AI infrastructure supercycle.

## The Fiscal 2024 Baseline

When KLA opened fiscal 2024 in July 2023, the memory downcycle imposed a visible constraint. DRAM and NAND customers had deferred equipment purchases, and foundry/logic — though incrementally healthier — was running below peak utilisation. Quarterly revenues ranged from approximately $2.36 billion in the March 2024 quarter, the cyclical trough, to approximately $2.57 billion in June 2024, for a [full-year total of $9.81 billion](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000319201&type=10-K) — a decline of roughly seven percent from fiscal 2023.

What the period demonstrated was the resilience of KLA's margin architecture under pressure. Services revenue, running at approximately $550 to $600 million per quarter, held consolidated gross margins in the 61 to 62 percent range throughout — an outcome that would have been unreachable in prior downturns, when equipment mix softness translated directly to consolidated margin compression. Management guided each fiscal 2024 quarter with approximately ±$125 million ranges; results came in at or near guidance midpoints, characterising a management team that preferred achievable over promotional forward estimates. These were not quarters of positive surprise; they were quarters of guidance discipline, and that discipline itself told investors something about management's epistemic honesty.

## The Fiscal 2025 Step-Change

The recovery in fiscal 2025 was foundry/logic-led and AI-anchored. Revenue rose in each of the year's four quarters: approximately $2.84 billion in Q1 (September 2024), approximately $3.08 billion in Q2 (December 2024), approximately $3.06 billion in Q3 (March 2025), and approximately $3.18 billion in Q4 (June 2025), for a [full-year total of $12.16 billion](https://ir.kla.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/500/kla-corporation-reports-fiscal-2025-fourth-quarter-and-full). GAAP net income reached $4.06 billion, or $30.37 in diluted earnings per share.

The guidance philosophy shifted alongside the revenue trajectory. Q2 and Q3 fiscal 2025 both came in above midpoint guidance as foundry/logic capex from TSMC and Samsung Foundry arrived earlier and in larger volume than conservative embedded assumptions. The pattern established what became the defining characterisation of KLA's investor communication during this period: management as deliberate underpromisers in a demand environment accelerating faster than their own public assumptions acknowledged.

## Revenue and Margin: The Eleven-Quarter Record

The table below presents the complete arc. Fiscal 2026 quarterly figures are as reported; fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2025 quarterly figures are approximate, derived from reported annual totals and disclosed quarterly trend data. Gross margins remained in the 61–62 percent range throughout the sequence.

| Quarter | Period Ended | Revenue | GM% | GAAP EPS | Non-GAAP EPS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 FY24 | Sep 2023 | ~$2.40B | ~61% | ~$4.79 | ~$5.89 |
| Q2 FY24 | Dec 2023 | ~$2.49B | ~61% | ~$5.27 | ~$6.16 |
| Q3 FY24 | Mar 2024 | ~$2.36B | ~61% | ~$5.00 | ~$5.26 |
| Q4 FY24 | Jun 2024 | ~$2.57B | ~62% | ~$5.29 | ~$6.60 |
| Q1 FY25 | Sep 2024 | ~$2.84B | ~61% | ~$6.20 | ~$7.33 |
| Q2 FY25 | Dec 2024 | ~$3.08B | ~62% | ~$7.43 | ~$8.20 |
| Q3 FY25 | Mar 2025 | ~$3.06B | ~62% | ~$7.05 | ~$8.02 |
| Q4 FY25 | Jun 2025 | ~$3.18B | ~62% | ~$8.16 | ~$9.00 |
| Q1 FY26 | Sep 2025 | $3.210B | ~62% | — | $8.81 |
| Q2 FY26 | Dec 2025 | $3.297B | ~62% | $8.68 | $8.85 |
| Q3 FY26 | Mar 2026 | $3.415B | ~62% | $9.12 | ~$9.30 |

*Sources: [KLA Corporation IR](https://ir.kla.com/financial-information/financial-results); [SEC EDGAR 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000319201&type=10-K). FY2024–FY2025 quarterly EPS figures are approximate; FY2026 figures as reported in earnings press releases.*

## 'Structural, Not Cyclical': The AI Demand Signal

The most consequential shift in KLA's earnings-call language during this period arrived at the Q2 fiscal 2025 call, covering the December 2024 quarter. Rick Wallace characterised AI infrastructure capital expenditure not as a recovery-phase tailwind but as a **structural** driver of semiconductor process control demand — distinct from the cyclical oscillations of DRAM and NAND spending that had defined prior industry cycles. The distinction carried valuation consequence: structural demand does not revert; it compounds. It justifies terminal multiples that cyclical demand cannot support, and it signals to analysts building long-cycle models that the current revenue base is a floor rather than a cyclical peak.

By Q2 fiscal 2026, as revenues reached $3.297 billion and set what was then a quarterly record, that framing had sharpened into explicit positioning. Wallace placed KLA at the centre of the AI infrastructure value chain:

> "KLA is a key enabler of the AI ecosystem."

The context was a quarter in which advanced-packaging inspection revenues — driven by TSMC's CoWoS and SoIC lines and SK Hynix's HBM3E and HBM4 stacking operations — were running at a pace tracking toward well above fiscal 2025's $925 million. Gate-all-around nanosheet process flows at 2-nanometre nodes, combined with hybrid-bonding tolerances demanded by multi-die chiplet assemblies, were generating more in-line inspection steps per wafer pass than any prior logic generation. The structural claim made six months prior was now evidenced by consecutive quarterly records.

## Segment Architecture: Where the Growth Originated

Below the consolidated line, three segments moved at different cadences. Semiconductor Process Control — the core, representing 90 to 92 percent of revenues — delivered the period's steady ascent from approximately $2.5 billion per quarter in fiscal 2024 to approximately $3.0 billion per quarter by mid-fiscal 2026. Broadband-plasma inspection tool shipments for TSMC N2 and Samsung SF3, alongside expanding Archer overlay-metrology deployments at every new lithography layer, drove the trajectory. SPC's compounding was structurally reliable: as node transitions multiplied the number of inspection-required process steps, KLA's content per wafer pass rose independent of absolute wafer volume growth.

Specialty Semiconductor Process — atomic-layer-etch and deposition systems for advanced packaging, MEMS, and power devices — produced the period's most variable quarter-to-quarter results, driven by large discrete-tool-shipment timing. OSAT customers accelerating chiplet-assembly capacity generated multiple outperformance quarters in fiscal 2025 before SSP normalised. PCB and Component Inspection, the Orbotech-derived segment, experienced a visible fiscal 2026 resurgence as AI-substrate orders from IC-substrate manufacturers in the CoWoS supply chain pulled forward direct-imaging and optical-inspection equipment purchases — lifting PCI from a modest contributor to a positive narrative that had been absent for most of the prior two fiscal years.

## The Services Anchor

Running through all three segments across the full period was the services business's compounding. From approximately $550 to $600 million per quarter in fiscal 2024, services revenue grew to approximately $625 to $650 million per quarter by fiscal 2026, marking fifty consecutive quarters of year-over-year growth. The increment appeared modest in percentage terms but was structurally disproportionate in its margin impact. Services gross margins structurally exceed the consolidated average; in any quarter where equipment revenues fell short of guidance midpoint — a large tool order deferred, a customer delaying final acceptance — the services line's stability prevented the consolidated gross margin from retreating below 61 percent. At approximately $2.5 billion annually and growing, the services base had reached the scale at which it could sustain the business through a moderate equipment-cycle correction without structural damage to the income statement.

## The China Headwind and Higgins' Arithmetic

No quarterly earnings narrative for this period was complete without the export-control overlay. From approximately 41 percent of revenues in fiscal 2024, KLA's China exposure contracted to roughly 30 percent in fiscal 2025 following successive rounds of U.S. Department of Commerce tightening. At the December 2024 investor call, CFO Bren Higgins quantified the incremental headwind from the most recent control tranche at $300 to $350 million for fiscal 2026 — a figure running, quarter by quarter, as a drag through revenues that would otherwise have comfortably exceeded the pace of fiscal 2025's acceleration. Taiwan, Korea, and the United States partially offset the displacement; TSMC and SK Hynix share gains absorbed a portion of the diverted China volume, though the arithmetic left fiscal 2026 carrying a visible constraint that would, in its absence, have made each quarter's beat pattern even more pronounced.

## Q4 Guidance and the Full-Year Calculus

For the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, management guided revenue of $3.35 billion plus or minus $150 million, with [GAAP diluted EPS of $8.85 plus or minus $0.78 and non-GAAP EPS of $9.08 plus or minus $0.78](https://ir.kla.com/news-events/press-releases/detail/509/kla-corporation-reports-fiscal-2026-second-quarter-results). Against the first three quarters' combined $9.922 billion, the guidance midpoint implied a full fiscal 2026 total of approximately $13.27 billion — squarely within the $13.2 to $13.5 billion range management had outlined at the March 2026 Investor Day, and approximately $1.1 billion above fiscal 2025's total.

The non-GAAP EPS run across the year — $8.81, $8.85, and approximately $9.30 in the first three quarters, followed by $9.08 at the Q4 midpoint — implied a full-year non-GAAP EPS of approximately $36 to $37, tracking ahead of the linear extrapolation required to reach $84 by fiscal 2030 but acknowledging that operating leverage at that scale would require continued revenue compounding rather than margin expansion alone. Wall Street consensus, clustered near the guidance midpoint as of the frozen date of this analysis, treated the $150 million guidance band as management's customary conservatism buffer — noting that in each of the prior three fiscal 2026 quarters, results had landed at or above the midpoint, producing the beat-and-raise pattern that had become the hallmark of KLA's investor communication and the primary argument for the premium multiple the stock commanded among its semiconductor-equipment peers.

chapters.title: The Long-Tenure Executive Team: Rick Wallace, Bren Higgins, and the Board That Governs a Near-Monopoly
chapters.body:
## The Engineer Who Stayed

Rick Wallace arrived at KLA Instruments in 1988 as an applications engineer — a title that, in the semiconductor equipment industry, means someone who goes into fabs, watches tools fail, and figures out why. He was twenty-six years old, held a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from the University of Michigan, and would spend the next eighteen years accumulating the kind of operational fluency that no corporate development curriculum can replicate. By the time the KLA-Tencor board named him President and Chief Operating Officer, and then President and Chief Executive Officer in January 2006, Wallace had worked through product line management, marketing, and business development at a company whose core physics — optical scatter, diffraction, and plasma-induced secondary electron emission — had barely changed since its founders commercialised the RAPID photomask inspection system in 1978.

The succession from Kenneth Levy, who co-founded KLA in 1975 and guided it through the 1997 Tencor merger, to Wallace represented a deliberate cultural continuity. Levy had built a company whose competitive identity was rooted in the conviction that process control was not a discretionary cost but a structural necessity — that customers who skimped on inspection spent more correcting yield problems than they saved on equipment. Wallace inherited that conviction and converted it into strategic doctrine. In the twenty years since his elevation to CEO, KLA grew from approximately $1 billion in annual revenue to a run rate exceeding $13 billion, navigated four industry downturns, executed the company's most transformative acquisition, and emerged from a period of U.S.-China export-control turbulence with its gross margins structurally intact above 60 percent.

Three strategic decisions in particular define the Wallace era. The first was the deliberate monetisation of the installed base through a services organisation that, by fiscal 2025, generated approximately $2.5 billion in annual revenue across spare parts, extended warranties, time-and-materials contracts, and Klarity software subscriptions — its fiftieth consecutive quarter of year-over-year growth. The second was the February 2019 acquisition of Orbotech Ltd. for $3.4 billion, which added printed-circuit-board and flat-panel-display inspection capabilities and, more consequentially, seeded the advanced-packaging inspection business that reported revenues exceeding $925 million in fiscal 2025. The third was the China export-control response: as successive U.S. Department of Commerce restrictions tightened between 2023 and 2025, Wallace redirected commercial energy toward TSMC, Samsung, and Intel Foundry, managing China's revenue share from approximately 41 percent of total revenue in fiscal 2024 to roughly 30 percent in fiscal 2025 while sustaining overall company revenue growth through the transition. The $26 billion, $84 non-GAAP EPS 2030 target model presented at the March 2026 Investor Day crystallised this multi-year repositioning into a public commitment that institutional shareholders could model.

## The CFO With an Unusual Portfolio

Bren Higgins joined KLA in 1999 and was named Chief Financial Officer in July 2013 after thirteen years in progressive finance roles within the company. His formal remit — finance, accounting, global manufacturing, logistics, supply chain, business development, and investor relations — is conspicuously broader than the scope most public-company CFOs hold. The organisational structure is not accidental. Following the supply-chain dislocations of 2020–2022, when semiconductor equipment lead times stretched to eighteen months and customers began placing speculative orders to secure allocation, KLA's management made a deliberate decision to elevate supply-chain visibility to the C-suite. Placing manufacturing and logistics under the same executive who manages the income statement and communicates with investors created a feedback loop in which inventory commitments, supplier agreements, and capacity planning became financially disciplined decisions rather than purely operational ones.

Higgins holds a bachelor's degree from UC Santa Barbara and an MBA in Finance from UC Davis. He and Wallace together represent a leadership pair with a combined KLA tenure of more than fifty years — a concentration of institutional knowledge in two individuals that institutional investors in the company's patient-capital shareholder base consistently cite as a differentiator relative to capital-light semiconductor equipment peers. Whether that concentration constitutes a succession risk or a competitive moat depends largely on the depth of the management layer beneath them.

## The Physics Architect and the Competitive Intelligence Import

Chief Technology Officer Ben Tsai spent more than thirty-five years at KLA and accumulated approximately fifty patents — a portfolio that spans the optical, e-beam, and computational inspection domains and represents the intellectual skeleton of the company's detection-sensitivity roadmap. Tsai is, by any reasonable measure, the single individual most responsible for translating the physics of defect detection into commercially deployed tool architectures. The concentration of foundational IP knowledge in one person is a governance risk that KLA has not addressed explicitly in public disclosures; the company's proxy statements and 10-Ks do not reference a named successor or a formal CTO-continuity structure, and Tsai's tenure — while an extraordinary source of competitive depth — creates a single-point-of-failure in a function where institutional knowledge compounds over decades.

Ahmad Khan, who carries the title of President, Semiconductor Products and Customers, joined KLA in 2004 following engineering roles at Applied Materials — KLA's most consequential process-control competitor. Khan leads the Semiconductor Process Control segment, which accounted for approximately 90 to 92 percent of total company revenues. His prior career at Applied Materials shaped the product-positioning vocabulary he uses in customer engagements and in public communications: on earnings calls, Khan speaks with unusual specificity about the application-level trade-offs between KLA's broadband-plasma optical inspection systems and competing tool architectures, a fluency that reflects direct competitive exposure rather than secondhand competitive intelligence. The combination of Tsai's physics depth and Khan's cross-competitor experience constitutes a product-strategy tandem that is difficult to construct organically.

## The Board: Industrial Credibility Without Private-Equity Distortion

KLA's ten-person board is chaired by Robert Calderoni, who served as Chairman and interim CEO of Citrix Systems and brings enterprise-software governance experience to a hardware-intensive business. The nine independent directors span a range of industrial and financial backgrounds that reinforces the thesis-level oversight of a near-monopoly in a physics-intensive sector.

| Director | Primary Affiliation | Relevant Background |
|---|---|---|
| Robert Calderoni (Chair) | Former Citrix Systems Chair/CEO | Enterprise software; board governance |
| Jason Conley | CFO, Roper Technologies | Capital-allocation discipline; technology holding structures |
| Tracy Embree | Former Cummins/Otis executive | Industrial manufacturing; global operations |
| Jeneanne Hanley | Former Lear Corporation SVP | Automotive supply chain; operational risk |
| Kevin Kennedy | Former Avaya CEO | Telecom infrastructure; technology transitions |
| Michael McMullen | CEO, Agilent Technologies | Test-and-measurement; semiconductor-adjacent equipment |
| Victor Peng | Interim CEO, PsiQuantum | Former Xilinx CEO; advanced semiconductor architectures |
| Jamie Samath | CFO, Intuitive Surgical | Medical device capital allocation; durable equipment businesses |
| Susan Taylor | Former Meta Chief Accounting Officer | Large-cap financial controls; technology sector |

Two board members warrant particular scrutiny from a governance standpoint. McMullen's simultaneous role as CEO of Agilent Technologies — a maker of test-and-measurement equipment with adjacencies to semiconductor process control — creates a potential conflict-of-interest surface that is disclosed in the proxy but not operationally disqualifying; Agilent and KLA compete at the margins of process-monitoring software and materials characterisation, not in the core patterned-wafer inspection market. Peng's interim CEO role at PsiQuantum, a quantum-computing startup funded in part by semiconductor-industry capital, reflects the board's appetite for frontier-technology exposure without introducing venture-style return horizons into KLA's governance culture.

Notably absent from the board is any private-equity or activist-investor presence. Institutional ownership is concentrated among Vanguard, BlackRock, and State Street — the passive, long-duration shareholders whose index-weight methodology rewards sustained earnings compounding over episodic financial engineering. This shareholder structure is reinforcing: it insulates management from short-cycle financial pressure, supports the long-duration R&D investment cycles that produced tools like the CIRCL-AP advanced packaging platform, and aligns the capital-return programme — $7.0 billion in supplemental repurchase authority authorised at the March 2026 Investor Day alongside a 21 percent dividend increase to $2.30 per quarter — with shareholders whose time horizon matches KLA's five-year target model.

## Compensation Architecture and the 2030 Alignment Question

KLA's executive compensation structure, disclosed annually in the DEF 14A proxy filed with the SEC, has historically weighted long-term incentives heavily toward performance share units tied to two metrics: non-GAAP diluted earnings per share and relative total shareholder return measured against the S&P 500 Information Technology Index. The structural question raised by the March 2026 Investor Day commitment to $84 non-GAAP EPS by 2030 is whether that target is now embedded in the PSU grant framework as a multi-year performance hurdle — a design that would align management incentives directly with the stated long-range model. KLA had not publicly confirmed such an embedding as of the frozen snapshot date, but the arithmetic is suggestive: a management team that announced a specific EPS target to institutional investors, authorised $7 billion in buybacks to support the trajectory, and raised the quarterly dividend by 21 percent in the same session has created accountability structures whether or not they are formalised in the proxy.

## The Succession Question

Wallace turned the CEO role in January 2026 — marking his twentieth anniversary as chief executive of a company he joined thirty-eight years prior. The question of leadership continuity at KLA is not academic. Wallace's technical fluency, relationships with the CEOs of TSMC, Samsung, and Intel Foundry, and institutional authority over the 2030 model are not transferable through a standard succession checklist. KLA has not disclosed a named successor, a CEO-in-waiting, or a formal timeline for Wallace's transition. The board's compensation committee oversees succession planning as a standing governance item, but the company's public disclosures treat the topic with the brevity typical of large-cap technology companies that have not yet been compelled by activist pressure or founder-transition circumstances to elaborate.
